Run long builds and scheduled jobs 24/7 on a remote Mac

Reviewed: 2026-11-21 · WodeMac

Long builds and scheduled jobs usually stop because of the host: a laptop sleeps, the Wi-Fi drops or the machine is busy with other work. Run them on a dedicated cloud Mac that stays online 24/7, keep interactive work in tmux, let launchd handle schedules and restarts, and write everything to logs, and the work continues after you close your own computer. Always on is not the same as never interrupted: power or network problems, a macOS update restart or a crashed process can still stop a job, so make jobs safe to rerun.

Jobs that belong on an always-on Mac

  • Full builds and test runs: a clean Xcode build or the whole test suite, which take long enough that you do not want them tying up your own computer.
  • Nightly jobs: pull the latest code, build, run regression tests and collect the reports at a fixed time every day.
  • Automation scripts: regular data syncs, status checks, batch processing of project files.
  • Anything that needs macOS: your team works on Windows or Linux, but the project needs Xcode or a macOS environment.

A job that runs once in a while and finishes in a few minutes is fine on your own computer.

Interactive work: keep it in tmux

A plain terminal opened over the remote screen or SSH can take its processes down with it when the connection drops or the window closes. tmux keeps the session independent of the connection. With admin rights you can install it with Homebrew:

brew install tmux
tmux new -s build        # start a session and run the build inside
# press Ctrl-b, then d, to detach; the job keeps running
tmux attach -t build     # come back later
tmux ls                  # list sessions

tmux only survives as long as the machine does. After a restart, tmux sessions and the jobs in them are gone, so anything scheduled or long-lived belongs in launchd.

Scheduled and long-running jobs: use launchd

launchd is how macOS runs background jobs. A plist file says what to run, as which user, when, and where to write output. Jobs in /Library/LaunchDaemons load at boot and do not need anyone to be logged in. This example runs a build script every day at 2:00 (replace dev with your user name):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.example.nightly-build</string>
  <key>UserName</key><string>dev</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array><string>/Users/dev/scripts/nightly.sh</string></array>
  <key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
  <dict><key>Hour</key><integer>2</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>0</integer></dict>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/dev/logs/nightly.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/dev/logs/nightly.err.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
plutil -lint com.example.nightly-build.plist
sudo cp com.example.nightly-build.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons/
sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.nightly-build.plist
sudo launchctl print system/com.example.nightly-build    # check status
sudo launchctl bootout system/com.example.nightly-build  # disable

For a long-running service, use KeepAlive instead of StartCalendarInterval and launchd restarts the process when it exits. The Mac is in California and its clock may be on US Pacific time, so check with date before picking a schedule. Steps that depend on a logged-in session, such as code signing or simulators, should be tested in the background before you hand them to launchd.

Logs, safe reruns and notifications

  • Log every run to a dated file, for example ./build.sh 2>&1 | tee -a ~/logs/build-$(date +%F).log.
  • Start scripts with set -euo pipefail so they stop at the first error instead of carrying on.
  • Make jobs safe to rerun: starting over after an interruption should not corrupt anything, or the job should skip steps that already finished.
  • Report success or failure at the end through something your team already uses, such as email or a chat webhook, so nobody has to watch the job.
  • Storage is 256GB: clear old logs, build output and Xcode DerivedData regularly and check free space with df -h, because a full disk fails jobs too.

What can still interrupt a job, and the cost

Online 24/7 means the machine stays powered on and connected, not that every job finishes. A power or network problem at the hosting site, a restart after a macOS update, a crashed process or a full disk can all stop work. After a restart, tmux sessions are gone and only launchd jobs come back. Make sure the logs show where a job stopped, and push code to a remote Git repository instead of keeping it only on this machine. For maintenance, WodeMac and the hosting provider keep admin access through DeskIn.

FAQ

Do jobs keep running after I shut down my own computer?

Yes. They run on the Mac in California, independent of your computer. Power or network problems, a system restart or a crashed process can still stop them, so log important jobs and make them safe to rerun.

Do jobs come back after the Mac restarts?

tmux sessions do not. Jobs managed by launchd in /Library/LaunchDaemons load again at boot: scheduled jobs run at their next time and KeepAlive services are restarted. Check the logs after a restart.

Is this a shared virtual machine?

No. Each physical Mac mini is rented to one customer, who gets admin rights. WodeMac and the hosting provider keep admin access for maintenance.

How much does it cost?

$169 monthly, $481.65 quarterly, $912.60 half-yearly or $1,723.80 yearly (about $143.65 a month), for the machine only, paid upfront for the chosen period.
